title: Authentication
subtitle: Watch a user prove who they are with a password, a session or token, an OAuth login, and a second factor.
learn: Why passwords are stored as slow salted hashes, never as text or fast hashes
How server-side sessions and signed JWTs differ, and what each costs you
The OAuth 2.0 / OIDC authorization-code login flow, hop by hop
How MFA adds a second factor and why phishing-resistant factors matter
How short-lived access tokens plus refresh tokens limit the damage of theft

steps.title: Who is this, really?
steps.body: HTTP has no memory: every request arrives as if it were the first. So when someone clicks Pay, how does the server know it is the same person who logged in a minute ago, and that they really are who they claim to be? Authentication means proving who you are. This lesson follows one login, from the first password to the tokens that keep you logged in.
steps.idea: Authentication proves identity once, then hands the client something cheaper to present on every later request.
steps.caption: A browser and an app server. Nobody has proved who they are yet.

steps.title: Check the password without keeping it
steps.body: You type your password and the browser sends it to the app over TLS (an encrypted connection). The app fetches your stored salt and hash from the user database. A salt is a random value saved next to the hash, so two users with the same password get different hashes. The app hashes what you typed with that salt and compares. The hash must be deliberately slow: Argon2id and scrypt are slow and memory-hungry, bcrypt is only slow. Aim for about 100 ms per check (a rule of thumb; never go below OWASP's minimum settings). A fast hash like SHA-256 lets attackers try billions of guesses per second. A match is not the end: MFA comes next.
steps.idea: Store a per-user salted slow hash. The server compares hashes and never needs to keep the password itself.
steps.caption: The app fetches the stored salt and hash, then compares.

steps.title: Option A: a server-side session
steps.body: Once login has fully succeeded (password plus any second factor, see the MFA step), the app creates a random 128-bit session ID. It saves the ID in a session store such as Redis, with the user ID and a 30-minute idle timeout. Then it sends the ID to the browser in a cookie marked HttpOnly (scripts cannot read it), Secure (HTTPS only) and SameSite (not sent on most cross-site requests). Browsers attach cookies automatically, so add anti-CSRF checks too. Each later request carries the cookie and costs one store lookup. To log someone out or ban them, delete their record.
steps.idea: A session is an opaque ID that points at data on the server. Revoking is instant, but every request costs a lookup.
steps.caption: App saves the session and sets a cookie. Each request then looks it up.

steps.title: Option B: a signed JWT
steps.body: Instead of keeping state on the server, the app can hand out a JSON Web Token (JWT). It holds claims (facts such as user ID and expiry) plus a signature made with a secret key. Any service can check the signature without calling a database. With public-key signing, services need only the public key, so they cannot forge tokens. The client sends the JWT as a Bearer token (whoever holds it is trusted). The catch: a JWT stays valid until it expires and is hard to revoke, so keep access tokens short, around 15 minutes.
steps.idea: JWTs trade revocability for stateless verification; keep them short-lived because you cannot take them back.
steps.caption: Signed token is checked locally: no store lookup.

steps.title: Log in with someone else's identity
steps.body: With "Sign in with Google", your app never sees the password. Your app redirects the browser to the identity provider (IdP), sending a random state value and a PKCE challenge (a hash of a secret the app keeps). The user logs in at the IdP, which redirects back with a short-lived, single-use authorization code. Your server trades the code, plus the original PKCE secret (the verifier) and its client secret if it has one, for an ID token (OpenID Connect, OIDC: who the user is) and an access token. Only the code travels through the browser. Your app then starts its own session.
steps.idea: OAuth/OIDC delegates the password to a specialist; your app only exchanges a one-time code for tokens over a back channel.
steps.caption: Redirect out, code comes back, tokens swap server to server.

steps.title: Add a second factor
steps.body: A password alone can be phished, guessed, or reused from another breach. MFA (multi-factor authentication) asks for something more: a one-time code from an authenticator app, a push approval, or a passkey (WebAuthn: a key pair kept on your device or hardware key). A passkey signs a challenge tied to the real site's domain, so a lookalike site gets nothing usable. SMS codes beat nothing but can be SIM-swapped (an attacker moves your phone number to their SIM). Here the app pauses the login, the browser asks the authenticator, and only then does the app issue the session or tokens.
steps.idea: Require a second, independent factor, and prefer phishing-resistant ones like passkeys over typed codes.
steps.caption: Login pauses until the second factor checks out.

steps.title: Stay logged in without long-lived access
steps.body: A 15-minute access token would log users out constantly, so login also returns a refresh token that lasts days or weeks. When the access token expires, the browser sends the refresh token and gets a fresh pair. Good practice is rotation: each refresh token works once, and if an old one is replayed the server revokes the whole chain, because replay suggests theft. The refresh token lives in a server-checked store, so it can be revoked (drawn here as the session store).
steps.idea: Short access tokens limit exposure; a revocable, rotating refresh token provides the long session.
steps.caption: Expired access token is swapped for a fresh pair.

steps.title: The user table leaks
steps.body: Suppose an attacker steals the whole user table. Because each password is a slow salted hash, they must guess one password at a time. At 100 ms per try that is only 10 guesses per second per CPU core. Attackers with GPUs and many cores multiply that, which is why weak passwords still fall. Salts stop one guess from checking every user at once. Plain text or unsalted MD5 would have exposed everyone immediately, and reused passwords would be tried on other sites.
steps.idea: Assume the database will leak one day; slow salted hashes plus MFA turn a breach into a slow, partial problem.
steps.caption: Attacker holds the hashes but must guess one at a time.

steps.title: The whole login
steps.body: Check the password against a slow salted hash, or delegate to an IdP with the OAuth/OIDC code flow. Add MFA, ideally a passkey. Then issue either a server-side session cookie, or a short-lived signed token with a rotating refresh token. Sessions make revoking easy, JWTs make verifying stateless, and many real systems combine both. What a logged-in user may do is authorization, a separate lesson.
steps.idea: Prove identity once with strong factors, then carry it in something short-lived and revocable.
steps.caption: Password or IdP, second factor, then tokens.

quiz.q: Why is bcrypt or Argon2id a better password hash than SHA-256?
options: It produces a shorter output that is cheaper to store
It is reversible, so support staff can recover forgotten passwords
It is deliberately slow and tunable, so brute-forcing a leaked table is expensive
It removes the need for a salt
quiz.why: Password hashes are deliberately slow (and, for Argon2id and scrypt, memory-hard) so attackers cannot test billions of guesses per second. They are not reversible, and salts are still used (usually built in).

quiz.q: A user reports their laptop was stolen and you must log them out everywhere right now. Which design makes that easiest?
options: Server-side sessions: delete the user's session records
Self-contained JWTs valid for 24 hours with no server state
Asking the user to change their password (existing sessions stay valid)
quiz.why: Sessions live on the server, so deleting them ends access immediately. A stateless JWT stays valid until it expires unless you add a denylist, which brings back server state.

quiz.q: In the OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow, why does the browser carry only a one-time code instead of the access token?
options: Codes never expire, so the app can retry later
The token is exchanged server-to-server with the client secret or PKCE verifier, so a code intercepted in the browser is useless alone
Browsers cannot store tokens at all
It lets the IdP skip authenticating the user
quiz.why: The code is short-lived and single-use, and redeeming it requires proof only your server (or the original client via PKCE) has, so the tokens never pass through the URL.

quiz.q: An attacker runs a fake login page that relays whatever the user types, including a 6-digit authenticator code, to the real site in real time. Which second factor best defeats this?
quiz.why: Passkeys sign a challenge bound to the genuine site's domain, so a lookalike domain gets nothing usable. Typed codes can be relayed by the phishing page.

cheatsheet.def: Random per-user value mixed into the password before hashing, so identical passwords hash differently and precomputed tables fail.
Slow, tunable password hashes. A common rule of thumb is roughly 100 ms per hash on your hardware; never go below OWASP's minimum settings.
Random opaque ID pointing at server-side state. Set HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite (and use CSRF checks). Instantly revocable, costs a lookup per request.
Signed token holding claims and an expiry. Verified without a lookup, but valid until it expires. Keep access tokens ~5-15 minutes.
OAuth 2.0 delegates access to resources; OpenID Connect adds an ID token on top that says who the user is. Use the code flow with PKCE.
Each refresh token is single-use and replaced on refresh; replaying an old one signals theft and revokes the chain.
A second independent factor. Passkeys (WebAuthn) are phishing-resistant because they are bound to the site's domain.
Authentication: who are you. Authorization: what may you do. Do the first, then the second, as separate checks.
